# How to use this book {.unnumbered}

## Conventions {.unnumbered}

Code you type and output you receive are shown in monospaced blocks. Where a block
shows a shell session, the command is given without a prompt character so that you
can copy it directly:

```{.bash}
seqkit stats data/sequences/sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.fasta
```

Blocks labelled with a language in braces — `{python}`, `{r}` — were executed when
the book was built, and the output beneath them is exactly what that code produced.
Blocks that are shown but not executed carry a note saying so, and their output was
captured from a real run and quoted.

Terms appear in **bold** at first definition and are collected in the glossary.
File formats are capitalised (FASTA, FASTQ, SAM, BAM, VCF, GFF3). Human gene
symbols are italic and upper case (*TP53*); the protein is roman (p53).

Five kinds of marginal note appear:

::: {.callout-note title="A definition or a pointer"}
Background, a format detail, or a cross-reference to where something is covered
properly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Something worth doing"}
A shortcut, a diagnostic command, or a habit that will save you time.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Something that will bite you"}
A step where people commonly lose data, waste days, or silently get the wrong
answer.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="An obligation"}
Ethical, legal, clinical or biosafety requirements. These are rare, and they mean it.
:::

Solutions to exercises are in a collapsed block at the end of each chapter. Open
them after you have tried the exercise, not before.

## Setting up {.unnumbered}

You need a Unix-like command line. On macOS and Linux you already have one. On
Windows, install the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2) and work inside it; a native
Windows installation will cause problems that this book cannot help you with.

Install [Miniforge](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge), then:

```{.bash}
git clone https://github.com/babasaraki/practical-bioinformatics
cd practical-bioinformatics
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate pablb
```

That single environment contains every Python package, R package and command-line
tool used anywhere in the book. Chapter 1 walks through the installation in detail
and verifies it.

## Getting the data {.unnumbered}

```{.bash}
python scripts/fetch_data.py
python scripts/fetch_data.py --check
```

The first command downloads roughly 12 MB from NCBI, UniProt, RCSB PDB, AlphaFold
DB, Bioconductor and STRING. The second verifies every file against the SHA-256
checksums in `data/MANIFEST.tsv`, so you know your copy matches the one the book was
written against. Appendix C lists each file, where it came from and what it is used
for.

Chapter code never contains a literal path. It calls a helper that locates the data
directory from wherever you are working:

```{.python}
from pybfx import book_data
book_data("proteins", "globins.fasta")
```

```{.r}
book_data("proteins", "globins.fasta")
```

## If something does not work {.unnumbered}

Check, in this order: that the environment is activated (`conda env list` shows a
`*` beside `pablb`); that you are in the repository root; that
`python scripts/fetch_data.py --check` reports no problems; and that your package
versions match those in `environment.yml`. If the problem persists, the issue
tracker on the repository is the right place to raise it, and a report that includes
the command, the full error and your `conda list` output will be answered much
faster than one that does not.

## For instructors {.unnumbered}

Each chapter is sized for one teaching session with the exercises as homework. The
worked solutions are part of the text rather than a separate instructor's manual, on
the view that students who look up an answer early learn more than students who
cannot check their work at all. The question bank in Chapter 16 is graded by
cognitive level and can be used for assessment. The whole book is openly licensed
for non-commercial use, so chapters may be adapted for your own course provided the
licence is preserved.
